q: Which Egyptian queen was the last active pharaoh of the Ptolemaic Kingdom?
note: She died in 30 BC, and Egypt was absorbed into the Roman Empire as a province.

q: What was the name of the large public square at the centre of civic life in ancient Rome?
note: Law courts, markets and public speeches all shared the same open ground.

q: Which Macedonian king conquered the Persian Empire and died in Babylon in 323 BC?
note: As a boy he was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle.

q: In ancient Rome, what kind of weapon was a gladius?
note: Roman foot soldiers fought at close quarters with it; the word gladiator comes from the same root.

q: In Greek legend, which city was besieged for ten years and finally taken by means of a wooden horse?
note: Heinrich Schliemann's 19th-century digs in northwestern Turkey are generally identified as the site.

q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon river with his army in 49 BC, triggering a civil war?
note: Bringing an army across that river toward Rome was, by law, an act of war against the state.

q: What is the name of the Roman defensive wall begun in AD 122 across northern Britain?
note: It ran roughly 73 miles coast to coast, and long stretches of it still stand.

q: Which Greek city-state trained its boys in a rigorous state system called the agoge?
note: Spartan boys entered the agoge at about the age of seven.

q: At which narrow pass did King Leonidas and a small Greek force hold off the Persian army in 480 BC?
note: The Greeks were finally outflanked by a mountain path revealed to the Persians by a local man.

q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to invade Italy in 218 BC?
note: He crushed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BC but never captured Rome itself.

q: Which Athenian philosopher was condemned to death in 399 BC and died by drinking hemlock?
note: He wrote nothing himself, so nearly everything known about him comes from his students Plato and Xenophon.

q: Who was the first emperor of Rome?
note: Born Gaius Octavius, he was granted the honorific name Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC.

q: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for which pharaoh?
note: It stood as the tallest structure built by humans for roughly 3,800 years.

q: Which ancient empire was founded by Cyrus the Great and later ruled by Darius I?
note: Cyrus is remembered for permitting exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return to their homelands.

q: Which Roman emperor, jointly with Licinius, issued the Edict of Milan in AD 313 granting toleration to Christians?
note: He later founded a new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium.

q: Which Chinese dynasty was founded by Qin Shi Huang, whose tomb is guarded by the Terracotta Army?
note: The buried army lay undisturbed until farmers digging a well uncovered it in 1974.

q: Which Athenian statesman led the city during the building of the Parthenon in the 400s BC?
note: The cultural high point of classical Athens is often called the Age of Pericles after him.

q: Which ancient people of southern Mesopotamia developed the wedge-shaped writing called cuneiform?
note: Cuneiform was pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus and stayed in use for some three thousand years.

q: Which Roman emperor wrote the Stoic private notebook known as the Meditations?
note: He wrote it in Greek, largely while on military campaign along the Danube frontier.

q: In what year is the Western Roman Empire traditionally said to have fallen, when its last emperor was deposed?
note: The deposed emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was still a boy and was allowed to live out his life on a pension.

q: In what year was the Battle of Hastings fought?
note: William of Normandy's victory permanently reshaped England's ruling class and its language.

q: What name is given to the plague that swept across Europe in the mid-1300s?
note: It reached European ports around 1347 aboard ships arriving from the Black Sea.

q: Which English king had six wives and broke with the Roman Catholic Church?
note: His break with Rome brought the Church of England into being with the monarch at its head.

q: Which charter, sealed by King John in 1215, placed limits on the power of the English crown?
note: It was sealed in a meadow at Runnymede beside the Thames, and John repudiated it within months.

q: Which French peasant girl led troops during the Hundred Years' War and was burned at the stake in 1431?
note: The Catholic Church formally declared her a saint in 1920, nearly five centuries after her death.

q: Which German monk's Ninety-five Theses of 1517 helped launch the Protestant Reformation?
note: His German translation of the Bible did as much to shape the modern German language as it did German religion.

q: Which city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, bringing the Byzantine Empire to an end?
note: The sultan who took it, Mehmed II, was only 21 years old at the time.

q: Which leader united the Mongol tribes and was proclaimed their ruler in 1206?
note: Under his sons and grandsons the Mongol realm became the largest contiguous land empire in history.

q: What was the name of the Spanish fleet that failed in its attempt to invade England in 1588?
note: Storms on the long voyage home around Scotland and Ireland destroyed more ships than the English navy did.

q: Which European war, begun in 1618, was ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648?
note: The Westphalia treaties are often cited as the beginning of the modern system of sovereign states.

q: Which queen ruled England from 1558 to 1603 as the last monarch of the Tudor line?
note: She died unmarried and childless, and the crown passed to James VI of Scotland, the son of her cousin.

q: Which English king was tried and executed in 1649 after losing the English Civil War?
note: England then spent eleven years without a monarch, governed largely by Oliver Cromwell.

q: Which Italian astronomer was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun?
note: He spent his last years under house arrest at his villa outside Florence, going blind but still writing.

q: Which French king, known as the Sun King, turned Versailles into the seat of his court?
note: His reign of 72 years is the longest of any sovereign monarch in European history.

q: Which family held the shogunate and ruled Japan from 1603 until 1868?
note: Their capital, Edo, was renamed Tokyo when imperial rule was restored in 1868.

q: Which wealthy West African empire was ruled by Mansa Musa in the 14th century?
note: His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was so lavish that it reportedly unsettled the price of gold in Cairo.

q: Which 1494 treaty divided newly encountered lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal?
note: The line it drew across the Atlantic is the reason Brazil ended up Portuguese-speaking.

q: Which Aztec ruler received Hernan Cortes when the Spanish reached Tenochtitlan in 1519?
note: Tenochtitlan stood on an island in a lake, on ground now occupied by Mexico City.

q: Which Byzantine emperor ordered the building of the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537?
note: He also had Roman law gathered and reorganized into the code that bears his name.

q: What name is given to the 15th-century English civil wars fought between the houses of Lancaster and York?
note: They ended in 1485 when Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth Field.

q: In what year did the American colonies adopt the Declaration of Independence?
note: Congress voted for independence on July 2 and approved the wording of the document on July 4.

q: Who was the first President of the United States?
note: He is the only president ever elected unanimously by the Electoral College, and it happened twice.

q: Which American founding document opens with the words "We the People"?
note: It was drafted in Philadelphia during the summer of 1787 and took effect in 1789.

q: Which US president issued the Emancipation Proclamation?
note: It took effect on January 1, 1863, and applied to the states then in rebellion.

q: What 1773 protest is remembered for colonists dumping chests of tea into a harbor?
note: The tea belonged to the British East India Company, and 342 chests went over the side.

q: What was the name of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to Plymouth in 1620?
note: Before going ashore the passengers signed the Mayflower Compact, agreeing to govern themselves by majority rule.

q: In which Pennsylvania town was the largest battle of the American Civil War fought in July 1863?
note: Lincoln's address dedicating the cemetery there, four months later, took about two minutes to deliver.

q: Which 1803 land deal with France roughly doubled the size of the United States?
note: The United States paid about 15 million dollars for territory spanning some 828,000 square miles.

q: What name is given to the period from 1920 to 1933 when alcohol was banned in the United States?
note: It ended when the Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth, the only amendment ever undone that way.

q: Which amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1920, gave American women the right to vote?
note: Tennessee cast the deciding 36th ratification, and the vote there turned on a single legislator changing his mind.

q: Which 1929 financial event is regarded as the start of the Great Depression in the United States?
note: The worst single day, Black Tuesday, fell on October 29, 1929.

q: What name was given to Franklin Roosevelt's program of relief and public works launched in the 1930s?
note: It built roads, dams, schools and post offices, and created Social Security along the way.

q: Which overland route carried thousands of settlers from Missouri to the Pacific Northwest in the 1840s?
note: Most emigrants walked the roughly 2,000 miles beside their wagons rather than riding in them.

q: Whose refusal to give up a bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955 set off a yearlong bus boycott?
note: The boycott ran 381 days and brought a young minister named Martin Luther King Jr. to national attention.

q: Which US state was bought from Russia in 1867?
note: At roughly two cents an acre the purchase was mocked at the time as "Seward's Folly."

q: Which British general surrendered at Yorktown in 1781, effectively ending the fighting in the American Revolution?
note: A French fleet and French troops were essential to sealing him off by land and sea.

q: Which 1803 Supreme Court case established the principle of judicial review?
note: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion claimed for the Court the power to strike down acts of Congress.

q: Which war was ended by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848?
note: The treaty transferred California and most of the present-day American Southwest to the United States.

q: Which 1854 act let settlers in two western territories decide the slavery question for themselves?
note: By undoing the Missouri Compromise line it set off the violent struggle known as Bleeding Kansas.

q: What is the name of the 1786 uprising by indebted Massachusetts farmers that alarmed America's founders?
note: It helped convince leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak, hastening the Constitutional Convention.

q: The assassination of which archduke in Sarajevo in 1914 helped set off the First World War?
note: He was the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his death triggered a chain of alliance obligations.

q: Which 1941 attack on a naval base in Hawaii brought the United States into the Second World War?
note: Congress declared war on Japan the following day, December 8, 1941.

q: What name is given to the Allied landings in Normandy on June 6, 1944?
note: Roughly 156,000 Allied troops came ashore or landed by air along fifty miles of coast that day.

q: Which wall divided a German city from 1961 until 1989?
note: It was opened on the night of November 9, 1989, after a muddled announcement at an East German press conference.

q: Which country launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957?
note: Sputnik was about the size of a beach ball and did little but circle the Earth emitting a radio beep.

q: Which ocean liner struck an iceberg and sank on its maiden voyage in April 1912?
note: Its wreck was not located until 1985, lying more than two miles down on the sea floor.

q: Which 1919 treaty formally ended the First World War between Germany and the Allied powers?
note: It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors on June 28, five years to the day after the Sarajevo assassination.

q: Which 1917 revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power in Russia?
note: It is called the October Revolution although, by the calendar most of the world uses, it happened in November.

q: Which Soviet city gave its name to the 1942-43 battle that turned the war on the Eastern Front?
note: The city has been called Volgograd since 1961.

q: Which war, fought from 1950 to 1953, ended with an armistice near the 38th parallel?
note: It closed with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the peninsula formally still at war.

q: What name is given to the October 1962 standoff over Soviet missiles placed on a Caribbean island?
note: The confrontation ran for thirteen days and is generally reckoned the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war.

q: Which 1938 agreement allowed Germany to annex the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia?
note: Neville Chamberlain came home waving the document and promising "peace for our time."

q: Which country did Germany invade on September 1, 1939, beginning the Second World War in Europe?
note: Britain and France declared war two days later, on September 3.

q: Which 1916 battle on the Western Front, fought along a French river from July to November, became a byword for trench warfare?
note: It was also the first battle in which tanks were used, though only a few dozen took part.

q: Which international organization was founded in 1945 to succeed the League of Nations?
note: Fifty nations signed its charter in San Francisco in June 1945, before the war had even ended.

q: In what year was the Soviet Union formally dissolved?
note: The Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin for the last time on December 25, 1991.

q: At which Crimean resort did Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet in February 1945 to plan postwar Europe?
note: Roosevelt was already gravely ill and died two months after the meeting.

q: Which 1957 treaty created the European Economic Community?
note: Six countries signed it, laying the foundation for what later became the European Union.

q: Which conflict of 1936 to 1939 ended with Francisco Franco in power?
note: Franco went on to rule Spain until his death in 1975.

q: Which war of 1904 and 1905 was settled by a treaty negotiated in Portsmouth, New Hampshire?
note: President Theodore Roosevelt won a Nobel Peace Prize for brokering the settlement.

q: Which British monarch reigned from 1837 to 1901, giving her name to an era?
note: She held the record as Britain's longest-reigning monarch until Elizabeth II passed her in 2015.

q: Which French emperor was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
note: He was exiled to Saint Helena, a speck of an island in the South Atlantic, and died there in 1821.

q: Which US president was elected to four terms and led the country through most of the Second World War?
note: He died in April 1945, weeks before Germany surrendered, and a later amendment capped presidents at two terms.

q: Which British prime minister led his country through most of the Second World War?
note: British voters turned him out of office in July 1945, before the war with Japan had even ended.

q: Which Indian independence leader built his campaign against British rule on nonviolent resistance?
note: His 1930 Salt March covered some 240 miles on foot to make salt from the sea in defiance of British law.

q: Which South African leader spent 27 years in prison before becoming his country's president in 1994?
note: He shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, the president who released him.

q: Which Russian ruler founded the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703?
note: He toured Western Europe in disguise as an ordinary workman to learn shipbuilding firsthand.

q: Which French king was on the throne when the French Revolution began, and was executed in 1793?
note: His wife, Marie Antoinette, was executed later the same year.

q: Which US president resigned from office in 1974?
note: He left the White House on August 9, 1974, and was pardoned a month later by Gerald Ford.

q: Which leader proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949?
note: He made the announcement from the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing on October 1, 1949.

q: Which Ottoman sultan, who came to the throne in 1520, was known in Europe as "the Magnificent"?
note: His own subjects called him "the Lawgiver" for his overhaul of the empire's legal code.

q: Which king was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in the year 800?
note: His biographer claimed he would not have entered the church that day had he known what the pope intended.

q: Which US president was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, in November 1963?
note: Lyndon Johnson took the oath of office aboard Air Force One at Dallas Love Field hours later.

q: Which Mughal emperor had the Taj Mahal built?
note: He built it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child.

q: Which Prussian statesman, nicknamed the Iron Chancellor, brought the German states together into one empire in 1871?
note: He engineered short wars against Denmark, Austria and France to pull the German states into line.

q: Which Soviet leader introduced the reform policies known as glasnost and perestroika in the 1980s?
note: The words mean roughly "openness" and "restructuring," and the policies loosened party control across Eastern Europe.

q: Which Italian leader led the red-shirted volunteers who helped unify Italy in 1860?
note: He landed in Sicily with about a thousand men and took the whole of southern Italy within months.

q: Which English queen ruled jointly with her husband William after they took the throne in 1689?
note: Their joint accession, which replaced her father James II, is known as the Glorious Revolution.

q: Which US president was the first to be impeached by the House of Representatives, in 1868?
note: The Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds needed to remove him from office.

q: Which Habsburg ruler governed Austria from 1740 to 1780 and was the mother of Marie Antoinette?
note: She was the only woman ever to rule the Habsburg lands in her own right, and she had sixteen children.

q: In what year did Christopher Columbus first cross the Atlantic and reach the Americas?
note: He made four voyages in all and went to his grave insisting he had found a route to Asia.

q: Which pair of brothers made the first powered airplane flight in 1903?
note: Their first hop at Kitty Hawk lasted about twelve seconds and covered less than the wingspan of a modern airliner.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
note: Buzz Aldrin followed him down the ladder about twenty minutes later.

q: Which German craftsman introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1450?
note: His famous Bible was printed at Mainz in the 1450s, and fewer than fifty copies survive.

q: Who received a US patent for the telephone in 1876?
note: Both his mother and his wife were deaf, and he spent much of his life teaching speech to deaf students.

q: Which canal, opened in 1914, links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
note: An earlier French attempt in the 1880s collapsed after enormous losses to disease and debt.

q: Which Portuguese navigator commanded the expedition that first sailed around the world, though he did not survive the voyage?
note: He was killed in the Philippines in 1521, and Juan Sebastian Elcano brought one ship home.

q: Which inscribed slab, found in Egypt in 1799, gave scholars the key to reading hieroglyphs?
note: Jean-Francois Champollion finally cracked the script in 1822, working from the Greek text carved alongside it.

q: Which British navigator charted much of the Pacific on three voyages in the 1760s and 1770s?
note: He was killed in a confrontation on a beach in Hawaii in 1779.

q: Which two men led the American expedition that reached the Pacific coast overland between 1804 and 1806?
note: A Shoshone woman named Sacagawea traveled with them as interpreter and guide, carrying an infant much of the way.

q: Which Norwegian explorer's party was first to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
note: Robert Falcon Scott's party arrived about a month later and died on the journey back.

q: Which Scottish engineer's improvements to the steam engine helped power the Industrial Revolution?
note: The unit of power used to rate everything from light bulbs to engines is named after him.

q: What was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869 when a golden spike was driven?
note: Two companies had been building toward each other for years, one east from Sacramento and one west from Omaha.

q: Which English naturalist published "On the Origin of Species" in 1859?
note: He had sat on the theory for two decades, and only a letter from a rival naturalist pushed him into print.

q: Which Polish astronomer argued in a 1543 book that the Earth travels around the Sun?
note: The book was published in the year he died, which spared him the argument that followed.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World was a lighthouse that guided ships into an Egyptian harbour?
note: It stood for roughly 1,600 years before earthquakes brought it down.

q: Which Chinese admiral commanded huge treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?
note: His fleets reached East Africa decades before Portuguese ships rounded the southern tip of the continent.

q: Which Norse explorer is credited in the sagas with reaching North America around the year 1000?
note: Norse ruins at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland confirm that Vikings did reach the continent.

q: Which Italian navigator gave his name to two continents?
note: A German mapmaker labeled the new lands "America" on a 1507 map, and the name stuck.

q: Which English doctor pioneered vaccination against smallpox in 1796?
note: The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin for cow, after the cowpox he used to confer protection.
